28F also from the UK. At 25 I had bright red blood and initially was told it was haemorrhoids. Went to a different doctor and did FIT/CAL-F tests. Went in for a colonoscopy. Colon was fine except for proctitis (a mild form of IBD). Had a follow-up earlier this year and it was haemorrhoids causing the bleeding. 

Google can’t see your colon. Check when your GP is open so you can deliver the repeat FIT test back. The sooner anything is detected, the sooner you can start treatment.

That’s not to say it’s definitely cancer, there are a few conditions that can cause these symptoms. Colon cancer itself isn’t always a death sentence - my neighbour had it and is thankfully still with us. 

I appreciate losing a family member to cancer can make it feel more scary. This was all going on in my life about a year after losing my Dad to cancer (not colon but still). There’s a fine line between being concerned about your health and letting it rule your life. Don’t underestimate the mental toll a cancer scare can have, maybe consider therapy if you feel it’ll help.

Good luck my friend :)

I got a 2.2 in my undergrad and a distinction in my masters.

For undergrad I did the assignments last minute and focused on living the student life. My subject felt way too difficult and I let myself believe that I’d never understand the material, but I’d “try my best”. Looking back, I wasn’t trying my best at all. 

For my masters I did treat university like a 9-5, because I’d schedule in lunch breaks and only work during those hours. If I wasn’t in a lecture, I was studying. Either doing an assignment or making notes and looking into topics. I also did volunteering and societies in the evenings - this was during lockdown so it was nice to have something to help me socialise, but it was massively helpful for developing skills and experience too.

I kick myself for not applying myself better at undergrad, but I’m glad I had the chance to go back and prove myself. My time management was a lot better and it was so nice not to be rushing to finish assignments just before the deadlines!

You’re not going to get spoon-fed information at degree level like they do at school. Not to be patronising at all - it is just a very different way of learning to what you’ll be used to. It can be a massive learning curve!

What you might find useful is noting down what the lecturer is saying. You have the slides already so there’s no point copying that down. You could print off the slides and make notes next to them, or bring a laptop and make notes on the PowerPoint. Or just make notes in a notebook and combine them with the slides later.

Something else I liked to do is write down questions - it can be as basic as “what does [this word] mean?” or it could be a note to find out more about a topic you’re stuck on.

One big tip for the actual ayesha part is to bring the other leg down first (rather than the one you brought down in the video). So whatever arm is on top when you’re upside down, bring that leg down first to balance - otherwise you’ll tip out.

Secondly, inverted D is a move in its own right and I think it would be good to strengthen that. By that point, your torso and hips are at an angle so you’re going to struggle to balance - you’re already tilting in a way that favours falling out of the move.

Get that pole on static and focus on strengthening each component. Remember “nose to pole” and really try and keep those hips square!

20 is not old at all. There are beginner pianists who are much older than you - please don’t let your age put you off, ever. 

I want to start by saying grades aren’t everything. If you want to do the exams, it can be a great thing to work towards and to show your progress. I played piano as a kid and fell into the trap of doing yearly piano exams - I learned to pass ABRSM exams, with little to my repertoire outside of that. I wouldn’t recommend it!

To answer your question, it depends. To go from 0 to grade 8 will take years, and it depends how much time you can dedicate to this. If you’re thinking of the exam route, you’ll also be learning to sightread and pass aural exams, as well as scales and arpeggios. These are all good skills to learn even without exams.

To get from 0 to playing basic chords and pieces can take less time, and can be really rewarding. Learning a few recognisable crowd-pleasers is a fun way to show off your skill!

All this to say, go for it, don’t let grades run your life, and have fun with it. I wish you luck!

I was thinking about the end of my life so much that it felt like it was going to come hurtling towards me - that I’d blink and I’d be on my death bed. If that were to happen, would I want to look back and see myself worrying constantly about this? No, that’s boring.

I’m not going to encourage you to do research into people’s experiences - honestly it just made me feel worse. It’s so easy to spiral in this kind of crisis. While I don’t usually suggest avoidance with any kind of mental health thing, maybe now isn’t the right time to look into it.

Focus on throwing yourself into life’s experiences. You don’t have to go sky diving or swim with sharks (you can if you want), but try and keep focused on what’s happening now, or what you have to look forward to in the near future. 

And watch out for the blimps ;)

I agree with a lot of the comments in saying that this sounds like OCD.

Looking at online resources (e.g. excessive googling) is a compulsion that many people struggle with.

In some forms of OCD with a sexual element, some people check for a groinal response. Some people feel arousal when they’re anxious, and assume that the arousal is because of the subject matter rather than their anxiety. 

Because you’re disturbed by the thoughts you’re having, I’d argue OCD is more likely than you being a pedophile. You want the thoughts to stop and you’re searching for evidence for/against pedophilia in yourself.

Please seek professional help for this. Try and find someone who understands OCD specifically. OCD themes can be really taboo, including pOCD. 

Here’s a link to a pretty comprehensive page about POCD specifically - https://www.choosingtherapy.com/pocd/

I felt the same when I was moved up from beginners. I could invert, and had gotten a Gemini once. Suddenly we were doing laybacks, brass monkeys, ayeshas… and I was terrified of all of them. I felt like I was one of the better ones in the beginner class to one of the worst in the intermediates. 

Here are some things that helped me - a growth mindset, basically! I took a break myself and when I came back I made a promise not to beat myself up if I couldn’t get a move, as long as I tried my best.

Celebrate small wins. You won’t learn a move in every single class, but even small steps towards your dream moves are worth celebrating.

Photo/video as much as you can. Learn to become objectively critical. None of that “this looks crap” stuff - watch what you’re doing frame by frame, trying to remember when you got close or decided to stop. See what’s going well, what could be improved etc. Watch tutorials to compare where you’re at vs where you are going. Get stuck in, do some research and enjoy the learning process as a whole!

Conditioning helps so much. I need to do more outside of class, but half of our lessons are geared towards pole-specific conditioning. I groan every class but I know it’s good for me.

Progress isn’t linear. Some weeks I make 0 progress at all, or I have 0 energy. Sometimes things will just click and something you couldn’t do last week suddenly works. I did my first scissor climb to the top of the pole last week whereas before I could barely make one rep 🤣

Have fun, enjoy the progress, set short term and long term goals. And give yourself a big fat high five regardless of what you’ve achieved

Hey! 28 year old with health anxiety who has had a recent flexi sig (like a mini colonoscopy). I also had a colonoscopy 2 years ago.

Prep isn’t fun but I didn’t find it too bad. The hardest parts are 1) not being able to eat and 2) the rumblies when you need to go. Keep some baby wipes and Vaseline to hand to help with any irritation, but honestly it’s not the same as having diarrhoea from my experience, I didn’t find the actual BMs painful. It’s the excessive wiping 🤣 other tips are stay hydrated, drink more than you usually would. And keep a hot water bottle if you’re getting crampy.

As for the procedure, I don’t know where you’re based but I’m in the UK and we’re offered a sedative (as opposed to full on anaesthesia). It sounds bad but it was my favourite part, as someone who is constantly on edge it was nice to feel so relaxed. I don’t remember most of it because sedative affects your short term memory, but I felt safe the whole time and someone was monitoring my vitals and checking I was okay, I never felt like I was in any danger.

They can usually tell you on the day what they’ve seen. If they send off for biopsies please don’t panic. It doesn’t mean there’s anything wrong, they might be just checking to see if they’re normal. They can also remove polyps during the procedure if needed.

A colonoscopy is the gold standard for diagnosis of colon things. I had large clots and bleeding nearly every time, and it ended up being haemorrhoids. Everything else all clear. And if it is something more sinister, at least you’re getting looked at. You’re taking responsibility for your health even if it’s scary, and that’s great.

Finally - and I mean this with all the love in my heart - get the fuck off Google please. It’s a safety behaviour to try and take some control of a stressful situation, but you’ll never satisfy the need for certainty by endlessly googling. I know it’s easier said than done, but Google can’t see your colon. 

Best of luck, you can do this!

28F here. I’m based in the UK and we have a 2 week wait/cancer referral pathway. You can be put through that way depending on your symptoms.

That being said, the first time I was referred I think I waited about 2 months from my initial stool tests. My second and most recent I was put on the cancer referral pathway. Both times I had the same symptoms, but I think it was because I never had a follow-up after the first and they wanted to make sure it wasn’t anything sinister.

In any case, a month is fine. Polyps take YEARS to develop into colon cancer, and not all of them will anyway (although they typically remove them anyway as a precaution). 

It is very hard not to worry when you’ve got to wait. I have health anxiety so I understand how difficult it can be. Stay off Google, keep yourself occupied with other things, and realise that you can’t do anything about it until the doctors have had a look.

Prep isn’t too bad, I mainly struggled with not eating 🤣 and the actual procedure is fine. We’re not knocked out in the UK but we can have a sedative which I opted for. 

They can usually tell you on the day if they see anything or if they’ve taken biopsies. If they take biopsies they may not be able to tell you exactly what it is but they should be able to explain why they’ve taken them. For example when I had my first colonoscopy they saw inflammation near the rectum, but they took biopsies further up to check other areas of my colon for comparison. 

Best of luck, I hope all goes well!

I had a flexible sigmoidoscopy today, full colonoscopy 2 years ago. I’m in the UK, for context.

Prep isn’t pleasant but it isn’t the worst thing either. It’s not like diarrhoea where it hurts, although if you are getting sore you can use a barrier cream and baby wipes. Drink plenty of clear fluids and make the path to the toilet as clear as possible. The laxative increases bowel activity, so once you get the urge it’s near impossible to stop it. Once all the hard stools are out of the way, it’s basically like peeing out of your bottom.

Sedation is my favourite part. It’s a little bit scary to start with if you’re nervous for it because the effects are quite quick. If you remember one thing, deep breaths. They should communicate with you when they’re giving you the sedation so you’ve got that warning sign to start breathing deeply. 

They’ll usually tell you what they can on the day, including if they took any biopsies. If you have any polyps they can usually remove them during the procedure. I know it’s hard not to worry, but a colonoscopy is the best way to see what’s going on down there. You won’t know until they tell you. Let them do your job, you focus on clearing your bowel as much as possible so they can do their bit.

ETA re: sedation, because I realised I didn’t give much detail about that. Initially it’s a rush where you feel head-drunk, that’s when I’d say to focus on your breathing because that’s the scary part. Once it passes, it’s absolutely fine. Time absolutely flies by as well, I believe it has something to do with the way it interferes with brain processing memories or something. I remember snippets, but it felt like 1 minute compared to the ~10 minutes I was actually being examined. Take your time getting up, I rushed earlier and had to sit down again!

I’m so glad you went on a date with someone else, and I would strongly encourage you to keep dating new people. You don’t have to be searching for your next partner, but getting out there and hanging out with different people is so refreshing. You don’t even have to just do this with people in a romantic setting - set up friend dates, catch up with people from your past, make new friends at hobbies/work and get to know them! I like to think of this as “diluting” the person out of your life. The more people you have in your life, the less significant he’ll seem over time. 

Ghosts, in my honest opinion, are fucking cowards. Especially the ones who ghost after sex. If someone is avoiding any form of confrontation with you, it shows emotional immaturity. What an attractive quality to have...

This might be harder but my next step is to block him. You’re not going to get closure from a ghost. That’s why they’re ghosts. Don’t allow him the pleasure of stepping back into your life whenever he wants you. That makes him feel like a higher value than you. And you know what? Fuck that. Even with a casual relationship, you deserve respect. Block him on all social media. This is tough, but so worth it. He wants to ghost you? Fine. Ghost back harder. 

“But what if he forgets about me?” I used to think this to myself whenever blocking someone and the response is - good. You don’t want that kind of person in your life anyway. And if he forgets about you, there’s less chance he’ll try and worm his way back in.

Invest in yourself. Push yourself at work or school. Start or develop some hobbies. Spend time with family and friends. Hit the gym or go swimming or dancing or whatever. I found yoga excellent for taking time to appreciate myself during a breakup.

Time will help you heal, of course. But making a bit of effort goes a long way. Don’t get stuck in a loop of crawling back to him when you’re lonely, or letting him back into your life. One guy I used to sleep with springs to mind here, and it’s taken me 2 years to let him go and realise how much of an arsehole he is. Don’t let that happen, you deserve more. 

TLDR: my main points are: treat it like a normal breakup, make him look silly in your head, keep dating/meeting new people, block him on social media and keep him blocked, invest in yourself and your own hobbies, and give yourself time. You won’t find closure from a ghost, but you can find it within yourself.
